--- title: Data annotation bibliography: ../course_refs.bib --- ::: {.objectives} #### Learning objectives * Define a subcellular marker, and explain why markers must be curated for the specific cell type and conditions being studied * Describe the iterative process of marker curation: select resolved compartments, source an initial list, evaluate, refine and annotate * Retrieve published marker sets with `pRolocmarkers()` and add published or user-defined markers to an `MSnSet` with `addMarkers()` * Evaluate markers visually using PCA and t-SNE across several principal components with `plot2D()`, marker profile plots and interactive visualisation using the `pRolocGUI` package * Quantify the separation of subcellular compartments with `QSep()` method, and interpret raw and normalised QSep scores * Refine a marker list by removing outlying markers and combining or removing poorly resolved compartments, without over-curating the data ::: ## Defining markers for machine learning In the context of spatial proteomics data analysis, a marker is a protein known to reside in a single subcellular niche within a given system *and* under given conditions. In other words, markers are proteins which we can confidently assign to a known single localisation based on prior knowledge. In the context of protein localisation prediction, marker proteins constitute the labelled training data provided to the classification algorithm. Defining marker proteins can be challenging and time consuming, but it is critical to obtain a list of markers which are representative of the experiment and dataset of interest. It is worth stressing at the outset that there is no single correct marker list. Marker curation is not a mechanical step with a fixed answer, but a series of informed decisions that depend on the biology of the system and the structure of the data. Which compartments are resolved, which proteins reliably represent them, and how much variation to tolerate within a compartment will all differ between organisms, cell types, experimental conditions and fractionation methods. A marker list that works well for one dataset may be a poor fit for another, even from the same organism. Two analysts working on the same data may also reasonably arrive at slightly different marker lists, and both may be valid, provided each decision is grounded in prior knowledge and supported by the data. The definition of subcellular markers can be broadly divided into five steps, with steps 3, 4 and 5 representing an iterative process, as outlined in Figure \@ref(fig:marker-curation). 1. Determine which subcellular organelles have been sufficiently resolved in the data 2. Generate or source an initial marker list for the selected compartments in your organism 3. Evaluate the suitability of the marker list for your specific dataset 4. Update the marker list by removing outliers, combining compartments or expanding markers 5. Carry out protein localisation classification using curated markers
::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![A graphical representation of the process of marker curation. Markers are proteins which are known to localise to a single subcellular compartment in the given cell type and condition of interest. The selection of confident markers is critical for successful prediction of protein localisation and differential localisation. (!) After using curated markers for protein localisation classification, users might still need to do some final curation e.g., if localisation prediction results do not look sensible (over- or under-classification of a particular organelle). However, users should be cautious when repeatedly refining markers lists as to ensure that the final markers remain representative of the literature and data structure.](figs/marker_curation.png){width=90%} ::: ::: Having visualised the data to validate the presence of clusters and explored which subcellular organelles may be resolved in the dataset, we can now start with an initial marker list. For model organisms, pre-existing marker lists can often be derived from published subcellular proteomics datasets. For simplicity, the `pRoloc` package stores a number of curated marker sets as well as published marker sets, as discussed below. However, for non-model organisms with limited pre-existing subcellular proteomics data it may be necessary to manually curate an initial marker list. In such cases we would advise users to apply unsupervised clustering to their data in order to guide marker discovery. ## Marker lists from `pRolocmarkers` The `pRoloc` package contains marker protein lists for a number of organisms, including curated organism reference sets and published marker lists. To see which marker sets are available we can use the `pRolocmarkers` function. Type `?pRolocmarkers` for more details. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## View available marker sets within pRoloc pRolocmarkers() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 14 marker lists (version 2) available: Arabidopsis thaliana [atha]: Ids: TAIR, 543 markers Drosophila melanogaster [dmel]: Ids: Uniprot, 179 markers Gallus gallus [ggal]: Ids: IPI, 102 markers Homo sapiens [hsap_christopher]: Ids: Uniprot, 1509 markers Homo sapiens [hsap_geladaki]: Ids: Uniprot, 579 markers Homo sapiens [hsap_itzhak]: Ids: Uniprot, 1076 markers Homo sapiens [hsap_villaneuva]: Ids: Uniprot, 682 markers Homo sapiens [hsap]: Ids: Uniprot, 872 markers Mus musculus [mmus_christoforou]: Ids: Uniprot, 922 markers Mus musculus [mmus]: Ids: Uniprot, 937 markers Saccharomyces cerevisiae [scer_sgd]: Ids: SGD, 259 markers Saccharomyces cerevisiae [scer_uniprot]: Ids: Uniprot, 259 markers Toxoplasma gondii [toxo_barylyuk]: Ids: ToxoDB gene identifier, 718 markers Trypanosoma brucei [tryp_moloney]: Ids: TriTrypDB gene identifier, 891 markers ``` ::: ::: We can see a number of lists, each labelled with species, ID type (UniProt protein accessions, species-specific gene IDs etc.) and the number of markers. The name of the marker set is indicated inside of square brackets. Reference marker sets for model organisms are named after their species: `atha` for the *Arabidopsis thaliana* reference set, `dmel` for *Drosophila melanogaster*, `hsap` for *Homo sapiens*, `mmus` for *Mus musculus*, and `ggal` for *Gallus gallus*. Marker sets extracted directly from publications are named using the nomenclature `species_author` e.g., `hsap_christopher` for the marker list used in @Christopher2025. To use one of the marker lists stored in `pRolocmarkers`, users should first extract the marker list into a named character vector by using the `pRolocmarkers` function and passing the name of the desired marker list. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Example extract markers from pRolocmarkers human_mrk <- pRolocmarkers("hsap") ``` ::: These markers can then be used to annotate the data via the `addMarkers` function, as demonstrated below. ## Adding user-defined marker lists It is possible to import and apply a user-defined marker list. The markers should be imported as either (i) a named vector where subcellular marker annotations are entries and feature accessions are the corresponding names, or (ii) from a `.csv` file with two columns, one for the subcellular marker annotation and another for the corresponding feature name. Of note, the feature names used in the marker list must be of the same format as those in the `featureNames` of the `MSnSet` to be annotated. In the use-case the format is UniProt protein accessions but `featureNames` could also be gene names or organisms-specific identifiers. We show how to load from a `.csv` file in the below code chunk and add annotation to the proteins in the data based on the marker list we have provided. A new column will be added to the data, which we will call "markers_initial". This is done by passing the argument `mcol = "markers_initial"`. For users who have extracted markers from `pRolocmarkers`, the code below should be edited to pass the extracted named character object (e.g., `human_mrk` generated above) to the `markers` argument. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Add markers to the MSnSet msn <- addMarkers(object = msn, markers = "data/dialop_markers.csv", mcol = "markers_initial") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Markers in data: 1725 out of 8736 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` organelleMarkers Actin Cytoskeleton Chromatin Cytosol Endosome 30 69 366 34 ER Golgi Lysosome Mitochondrion 231 38 36 346 Nucleus Peroxisome PM Proteasome 402 17 82 28 Ribosome 40S Ribosome 60S unknown 14 32 7011 ``` ::: ::: Upon successfully annotating the markers, a table is printed to the screen summarising the number of markers that have been added to the data. We see a new column has been added to the `fData` of our `MSnSet` to annotate these proteins in our dataset, called "markers_initial". ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Print the column names of the fData msn |> fvarLabels() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Channel" "Decoy" "Proteotypic" [4] "Protein.Ids" "Protein.Group" "Protein.Names" [7] "Genes" "PG.TopN" "Genes.TopN" [10] "Translated.Q.Value" "Channel.Q.Value" "Lib.PG.Q.Value" [13] "is_contaminant" "n_rep1" "n_rep2" [16] "n_rep3" "n_min" "n_mean" [19] "missing_rep1" "missing_rep2" "missing_rep3" [22] "missing_max" "missing_mean" "hc" [25] "hdb_cluster_id" "hdb_cluster_prob" "markers_initial" ``` ::: ::: If you wish to remove the markers from your data you can assign NULL to the output i.e., one would type `fData(msn)[, "markers_initial"] <- NULL` to remove the marker list. Additionally, if you wish to use a different name to "markers", to refer to your annotation list users can pass a new name using the argument `mcol` when using `addMarkers`. See the help documentation of `addMarkers` by typing `?addMarkers` for more details. ::: {.callout-note} #### An additional note on minimum number of markers per compartment Determining the optimal number of markers to include in the training data can be challenging. The inclusion of more training data (markers) is usually thought to increase the generalisability of a model, although this is only true if these markers represent the full diversity of data and do not lead to model over-fitting. While there are no fixed rules on the minimum number of training examples needed to learn a classifier, we suggest (1) having a sufficient number of markers per class to run cross-validation e.g. 10-15 for a 5-fold cross validation, (2) more markers than quantitation features e.g. for correlation profiling experiment with 10 abundance channels, > 10. Some classifiers also require the number of examples per class to be balanced. Unfortunately, the number of proteins known to reside in a subcellular niche can vary greatly, and some niches simply have too few proteins to add more markers. For example, the peroxisome is a relatively small organelle with few available marker proteins. This means that for experiments with many fractions and multiple replicates it may not be possible to have the number of peroxisomal markers exceed the number of quantitative channels. Nevertheless, users should be aware of these general guidelines and try to meet them where possible. ::: ## Evaluating markers After annotating the markers we again use dimensionality reduction within the `plot2D` function as a visualisation tool. This time we pass `fcol = "markers_initial"` to colour our proteins based on the `markers_initial` column within our `fData`. As outlined above, we expect markers to cluster together on these 2D plots. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(2, 1)) plot2D(msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers_initial", main = "Initial marker resolution PCA") addLegend(msn, where = "bottomright", fcol = "markers_initial", cex = .7) set.seed(399) plot2D(msn, method = "t-SNE", fcol = "markers_initial", main = "Initial marker resolution t-SNE") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Loading required namespace: Rtsne ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} addLegend(msn, where = "bottomright", fcol = "markers_initial", cex = .7) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P2_02_marker_annotation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: As expected, the majority of markers cluster together with other proteins from the same subcellular compartment. However, we can see some protein markers which do not cluster as tightly with the rest of their compartment. Additionally, whilst the t-SNE plot shows all clusters to be relatively well separated, the PCA plot displays an overlap between the ER (dark green) and plasma membrane (light green). This is because the `plot2D` function uses PC1 and PC2 by default which limits visualisation to compartments resolved in these first two dimensions. We can pass a vector of alternative PC dimensions to the `dims` argument within `plot2D` to explore resolution in these lower PCs. Below we show that the ribosome compartments, Golgi and lysosome are better differentiated when visualised with other PCs. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(2, 2)) ## Visualise PC1 and PC2 - the PCs which explain the most variance in our data plot2D(msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers_initial", main = "Marker resolution in PC1 and PC2") addLegend(msn, where = "bottomright", fcol = "markers_initial", cex = .7, ncol = 2) ## Visualise PC2 and PC3 plot2D(msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers_initial", dims = c(2, 3), main = "Marker resolution in PC2 and PC3") ## Visualise PC1 and PC3 plot2D(msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers_initial", dims = c(1, 3), main = "Marker resolution in PC1 and PC3") ## Visualise PC3 and PC4 plot2D(msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers_initial", dims = c(3, 4), main = "Marker resolution in PC3 and PC4") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P2_02_marker_annotation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: Importantly, although dimensionality reduction provides a convenient visualisation tool, neither the PCA nor the t-SNE co-ordinates represent the data input for downstream supervised machine learning classification algorithms. The training data for classification are the marker protein correlation profiles. Therefore, it is critical to look directly at these profiles as well as the 2D maps. The `plotDist` function within `pRoloc` generates a line plot showing the protein distribution profiles. We pass our `msn` object and subset the proteins annotated as `"Mitochondrion"` in the `markers_initial` column of the `fData`. Check the marker names in the data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} getMarkerClasses(msn, fcol = "markers_initial") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Actin Cytoskeleton" "Chromatin" "Cytosol" [4] "Endosome" "ER" "Golgi" [7] "Lysosome" "Mitochondrion" "Nucleus" [10] "Peroxisome" "PM" "Proteasome" [13] "Ribosome 40S" "Ribosome 60S" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Subset mitochondrial markers mt <- fData(msn)$markers_initial == "Mitochondrion" ## Plot the distributions of mitochondrial markers plotDist(object = msn[mt, ], pcol = "#A65628", las = 2) title("Mitochondrial markers") ``` ::: A `for` loop can be used to plot the distribution of each marker class, as outlined in the code chunk below. The `getMarkerClasses` function can be used to return a vector of all subcellular marker compartments in a given `MSnSet`. ::: {.cell layout-align="10"} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Define marker compartments marker_organelles <- getMarkerClasses(msn, fcol = "markers_initial") ## Define colours my_cols <- getStockcol() ## Plot marker distribution profile per compartment par(mfrow = c(4, 4)) for (i in 1:length(marker_organelles)) { marker_indices <- fData(msn)$markers_initial == marker_organelles[i] plotDist(msn[marker_indices, ], pcol = my_cols[i], xlab = "Fraction", ylab = "Intensity") title(marker_organelles[i]) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P2_02_marker_annotation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='10' width=960} ::: ::: Plotting the concatenated profiles is useful as it allows us to assess the suitability of markers across all three replicates at once. Importantly, a protein can only be considered to be a marker if it behaves as such across all replicates. Overall, this marker set is a good fit to the data. Nevertheless, there are a few markers that could be removed. ::: {.callout-note} #### An additional note on outlier marker removal Decisions regarding what constitutes an "outlier marker" can be challenging. In most correlation profiling experiments the marker profiles will contain a certain degree of noise, and this is to be expected. Further, the degree of noise will differ across subcellular compartments depending upon how well they behave during the biochemical fractionation process. For instance, in the use-case data the proteasomal markers have a very tight profile with minimal noise whilst the nuclear markers have a wider profile indicating more variation in the behaviour of these proteins during fractionation. Whilst it would be possible to extract a subset of nuclear markers to generate a much tighter set of profiles (which would translate to a tighter cluster when visualised via dimensionality reduction), this would be an inaccurate representation of the data. Indeed, over-curation of markers to generate unrealistically tight clusters can lead to over-fitting of downstream protein localisation classification models. In other words, the nuclear markers would no longer be a true representation of the nucleus and the model may fail to recognise which of our unknown proteins should be classified as nuclear. The goal of marker curation is to select a set of markers which accurately represent the dataset being analysed. Moreover, some machine learning models are more robust to outliers than others. ::: ## Quantifying resolution using `QSep` In addition to identifying outlying markers in each of the annotated compartments, users should also consider whether all of the initial compartments have sufficient resolution to be included in downstream classification. From the marker plots generated above, the initial compartments in our marker set do seem to be reasonably well resolved. However, we can take a more quantitative approach to exploring resolution by using the `QSep` function within `pRoloc`. `QSep` is a method for quantifying the separation of clusters in subcellular spatial proteomics datasets [@Gatto2019]. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Carry out QSep qsep_res <- QSep(object = msn, fcol = "markers_initial") ## Verify qsep_res ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Object of class 'QSep'. Data: msn With 14 sub-cellular clusters. ``` ::: ::: The `QSep` function returns a specialised object of class `QSep`. Within this object we can access matrices containing two types of QSep score: (1) the original and (2) normalised QSep scores. Original QSep scores are calculated as the average Euclidean distance between two clusters and thus directly quantify how far apart the clusters are when visualised via PCA. These scores are calculated using one of the clusters as a reference cluster. Since the distance between two clusters is the same regardless of which is the reference, the original QSep scores will be a symmetrical matrix. We can access this matrix by executing `qsep_res@x`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Look at original QSep scores qsep_res@x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Cytosol ER Mitochondrion QSep scores, a higher score indicates better resolution between clusters. We can also visualise the results of QSep in multiple ways. Firstly, the `plot` function within the `pRoloc` package can be used to generate a boxplot of the QSep scores for each included compartment. The `norm` argument takes a logical input to indicate whether to use normalised or raw QSep scores. ::: {.cell layout-align="5"} ```{.r .cell-code} par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) ## Plot a boxplot of raw QSep scores plot(x = qsep_res, norm = FALSE) title("Raw QSep scores for initial markers") ## Plot a boxplot of normalised QSep scores plot(x = qsep_res, norm = TRUE) title("Normalised QSep scores for initial markers") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P2_02_marker_annotation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='5' width=1152} ::: ::: From these boxplots we are able to see which of our subcellular compartments have higher overall normalised QSep scores, thus indicating that they are well resolved. In the use-case data, chromatin, mitochondrion, and lysosome are our three most well-resolved compartments. Secondly, to take a closer look at the pairwise QSep scores we can use the `levelPlot` function, again with the `norm` argument to specify which type of score we are interested in. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Plot a level plot of raw QSep values between each compartment levelPlot(object = qsep_res, norm = FALSE, main = "Raw QSep values for initial markers") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P2_02_marker_annotation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Plot a level plot of normalised QSep values between each compartment levelPlot(object = qsep_res, norm = TRUE, main = "Normalised QSep values for initial markers") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P2_02_marker_annotation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Looking at the pairwise QSep scores is particularly useful in identifying which subcellular compartments are the least resolved from each other. In the use-case data the ribosomes have the lowest pairwise resolution, some of this may be down to the annotation of individual subunits and class labelling. When resolution between two subcellular compartments is low (i.e., their pairwise QSep scores are low) there is a higher chance of proteins being misclassified between these compartments during downstream machine learning. Indeed, a subcellular compartment could have a high average QSep score, but the ability to correctly classify proteins to that compartment is determined almost entirely by its lowest pairwise QSep score. For compartments where all calculated QSep scores are low, users may consider whether it is appropriate to include the compartment at all or combine them with other classes under one umbrella term, for example here we could combine the 40S and 60S subunits into one term "Ribosome". By contrast, for compartments with high overall scores but one or two low pairwise QSep scores it may be worth combining the compartments with lower resolution. After making any changes, QSep scores can be recalculated on the updated annotated `MSnSet` to determine whether resolution has been improved. QSep scores are a quantitative measure of cluster (subcellular compartment) separation. Higher QSep scores indicate that clusters are more well resolved from each other. However, users should not aim for unreasonably high QSep scores. As discussed above in "An additional note on outlier marker removal", over-curation can generate unrealistically tight protein clusters which are no longer representative of the dataset. These clusters would have relatively higher QSep scores, since they are tighter and further separated from other compartments, but could still lead to over-fitting during protein localisation classification. ## Interactive data visualisation Visual exploration of correlation profiling datasets is a key aspect of the data analysis. As outlined above, the visualisation of marker protein distribution profiles as well as the annotation of these proteins on 2D maps facilitates the marker curation process required prior to protein localisation classification. To make this process of visual data exploration easier and reduce the need for excess plotting, the `pRolocVis` function from the [`pRolocGUI`](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/pRolocGUI.html) package can be used. We simply pass our `MSnSet` object to the `pRolocVis` function, specify a method of dimensionality reduction and a column from our `fData` which we wish to visualise, here the `markers_initial` column. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Open pRolocGUI pRolocVis(object = msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers_initial") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Screenshot of the pRolocVis GUI application.](figs/pRolocVis_screenshot.png){width=80%} ::: ::: Using this interactive visualisation tool (Figure \@ref(fig:pRolocvis-picture)) enables us to easily identify which proteins the outlier points and profiles correspond to. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Example steps for identifying outlier with pRolocVis.](figs/curation_example.png){width=100%} ::: ::: In the example above we identify a clear endosomal outlier. We see Q7LBR1 is annotated as endosomal (orange) and does not cluster with the other endosomal markers. We can use the `pRolocVis` app to identify this protein and also check its correlation profile. We indeed see its profile does not fit the average profile of the endosomal markers. For this reason we note this protein as not a good candidate for an endosomal marker in this dataset. ::: {.callout-exercise} #### Challenge: Identifying the actin markers **Task 1** Use `getMarkers` to find out how many actin cytoskeleton markers there are in this marker list. **Task 2** Use the `pRolocVis` app from the `pRolocGUI` package to examine the profiles of the actin markers, or the `plotDist` function. Do you think they should be included as a marker class for downstream machine learning analysis? **Task 3** Extract the UniProt accession numbers of the actin cytoskeleton markers and store them in your R notebook or `character` `vector`. ::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"} **Task 1** The `getMarkers` function prints a summary table of the number of markers per class in the dataset. The column "`markers_initial`" contains the current markers we are working with. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} getMarkers(msn, fcol = "markers_initial") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` organelleMarkers Actin Cytoskeleton Chromatin Cytosol Endosome 30 69 366 34 ER Golgi Lysosome Mitochondrion 231 38 36 346 Nucleus Peroxisome PM Proteasome 402 17 82 28 Ribosome 40S Ribosome 60S unknown 14 32 7011 ``` ::: ::: **Task 2** Using the `plotDist` function. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Subset actin cytoskeleton markers actin <- fData(msn)$markers_initial == "Actin Cytoskeleton" ## Plot the distributions of actin cytoskeleton markers plotDist(object = msn[actin, ], pcol = "red", las = 2) title("Actin cytoskeleton markers") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P2_02_marker_annotation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: You could have also used the `pRolocVis` function and selected the "Profiles" tab to examine the actin markers. **Task 3** There are several ways to do this, one way - ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ind <- which(fData(msn)$markers_initial == "Actin Cytoskeleton") actin_names <- featureNames(msn)[ind] actin_names ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "O15143" "O15144" "O15145" "O15511" "O75369" "P06753" "P09493" "P12814" [9] "P13796" "P23528" "P28289" "P47755" "P47756" "P52907" "P59998" "P61158" [17] "P61160" "P63261" "Q01518" "Q14847" "Q16658" "Q562R1" "Q92747" "Q9BPX5" [25] "Q9BR76" "Q9NYL9" "Q9NZ32" "Q9UJW0" "Q9Y281" "Q9Y4G6" ``` ::: ::: ::::: ::: ::: {.callout-important} #### Marker curation requires judgement In the next section we refine our marker list, and in doing so we make a series of choices: which outliers to remove, which compartments to keep and which classes to combine or drop. None of these choices is black and white, and there are several sensible ways to approach each one. For example, you might: * keep a noisy compartment because it is biologically important, or remove it because it is poorly resolved * combine closely related compartments into one broader class, or keep them separate to gain finer detail at the cost of more misclassification * remove an outlying marker, or keep it because it reflects genuine variation within that compartment The right choice depends on the organism, cell type, experimental conditions and the question you want to answer. What matters is that each decision is deliberate, justified by prior knowledge and the data, and recorded so that it can be reported and reproduced. This care is worth taking because markers are the training data for every downstream step. A supervised classifier can only learn the compartments, and the boundaries between them, that the markers define. Any errors or biases in the marker list are carried directly into the predicted localisations, and from there into differential localisation analysis. ::: ## Refining marker lists Having made an assessment of the suitability of our initial marker list, we can now update our marker list accordingly. There are three different aspects to consider here: 1. Removal of outlier markers 2. Combining compartments which lack sufficient resolution 3. Expansion or removal of marker compartments which have an insufficient number of proteins to use as training data for classification With respect to removing the annotation for individual outlier proteins, we previously visualised the correlation profiles of each marker compartment and used `pRolocGUI` to interactively identify which proteins the outlier profiles belong to. As we wish to keep track of marker annotation throughout our analysis we create a new column for our final marker list that we will use for analysis. We will call this "markers". This is the default value of the `fcol` argument in `pRoloc` for many of `pRoloc`'s functions. This means we can omit `fcol` in many arguments. Let's first create this new list, ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fData(msn)$markers <- fData(msn)$markers_initial ``` ::: Check it's been created, ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} msn |> fvarLabels() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Channel" "Decoy" "Proteotypic" [4] "Protein.Ids" "Protein.Group" "Protein.Names" [7] "Genes" "PG.TopN" "Genes.TopN" [10] "Translated.Q.Value" "Channel.Q.Value" "Lib.PG.Q.Value" [13] "is_contaminant" "n_rep1" "n_rep2" [16] "n_rep3" "n_min" "n_mean" [19] "missing_rep1" "missing_rep2" "missing_rep3" [22] "missing_max" "missing_mean" "hc" [25] "hdb_cluster_id" "hdb_cluster_prob" "markers_initial" [28] "markers" ``` ::: ::: In the below code we remove the annotation for the following outlying proteins in our new `markers` column, - "Q7LBR1" is labelled as endosome but sits away from the rest of the endosomal markers. - "Q8NBJ9", "Q9NUN5" are annotated to the lysosome but do not cluster with the other lysosomal markers. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Screenshots of the pRolocVis app with endosomal and lysosomal markers highlighted.](figs/pRolocVis_mrk_end_lys.png){width=100%} ::: ::: In the below code chunk we define the markers to be renamed. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Define marker accessions identified as outliers outlier_acc <- c("Q7LBR1", "Q8NBJ9", "Q9NUN5") ## Convert 'marker' column to unknown to_rm <- which(fData(msn)$Protein.Group %in% outlier_acc) fData(msn)$markers[to_rm] <- "unknown" ``` ::: We can validate the removal of these 3 proteins by looking at a table of the markers using the `getMarkers` function. We see that previously we had 7011 "unknown" (unannotated) proteins, and now we have 7014. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} getMarkers(msn, fcol = "markers_initial") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` organelleMarkers Actin Cytoskeleton Chromatin Cytosol Endosome 30 69 366 34 ER Golgi Lysosome Mitochondrion 231 38 36 346 Nucleus Peroxisome PM Proteasome 402 17 82 28 Ribosome 40S Ribosome 60S unknown 14 32 7011 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} getMarkers(msn, fcol = "markers") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` organelleMarkers Actin Cytoskeleton Chromatin Cytosol Endosome 30 69 366 33 ER Golgi Lysosome Mitochondrion 231 38 34 346 Nucleus Peroxisome PM Proteasome 402 17 82 28 Ribosome 40S Ribosome 60S unknown 14 32 7014 ``` ::: ::: Next, we consider whether to remove any compartment annotation and leave these proteins as "unknown" or "unlabelled". Visualisation of PCA and t-SNE plots and QSep analysis showed good overall resolution of the marker classes, with median normalised between-cluster distances of about 2–5 for all compartments. Mitochondrion and chromatin were the best-resolved classes, with the largest raw distances to other compartments (median about 1.15–1.2) and high normalised scores (median about 4–5). The mitochondrial markers also formed the tightest cluster (within-cluster distance about 0.15). In contrast, the actin cytoskeleton class was poorly defined. It had one of the most diffuse marker clusters (within-cluster distance about 0.48, second only to Chromatin) and, together with endosome, the shortest median distance to other compartments (about 0.7). Because its markers are both dispersed and close to the other compartments, the class does not form a distinct cluster and is likely to cause unreliable classifications. We therefore decide to remove it from the marker set. This is a judgement call rather than the only correct answer. A researcher whose question centres on the actin cytoskeleton might reasonably choose to keep the class, accepting that classifications to it will be less certain and interpreting them with appropriate caution. Should users wish to remove the annotation for an entire compartment, the `fDataToUnknown` function provides an easy way to achieve this. We pass our `MSnSet`, the `"markers"` column and then use the `from` and `to` arguments to change our annotations `from` a given organelle `to` `"unknown"` (the default), or another annotation if desired, as shown below. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Change actin to "unknown" in the column "markers" msn <- fDataToUnknown(object = msn, fcol = "markers", from = "Actin Cytoskeleton", to = "unknown") ## We see the actin annotation has been removed and relabelled as "unknown" getMarkers(msn) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` organelleMarkers Chromatin Cytosol Endosome ER Golgi 69 366 33 231 38 Lysosome Mitochondrion Nucleus Peroxisome PM 34 346 402 17 82 Proteasome Ribosome 40S Ribosome 60S unknown 28 14 32 7044 ``` ::: ::: Similarly, this function can also be used to change the names of compartments, replacing "unknown" in the above code chunk to the desired compartment name. Finally, if users find that their initial or curated marker lists include compartments of interest which appear to be sufficiently resolved but have too few marker proteins (see the note "An additional note on minimum number of markers") it may be necessary to find some additional marker proteins within the dataset. This could be informed by the results of unsupervised clustering, as demonstrated in the last lesson. Alternatively, users could consider looking at different marker sets to see whether there are any other well-established marker proteins for their compartment of interest. After updating the marker list, users are advised to re-plot the marker profiles and annotated dimensionality reduction plots to display the final markers. This can be achieved using the same code as above, so for the simplicity of this workflow we will not repeat the plotting here. ::: {.callout-exercise} #### Challenge: Re-assess the curated markers Marker curation is iterative, so after refining the marker list we should check whether our changes have improved the fit of the markers to the data. **Task 1** Re-run `QSep` using the curated `markers` column and store the result in a new object called `qsep_final`. **Task 2** Plot the normalised QSep scores for the initial and the curated markers side by side, both as boxplots and as level plots. Has the separation of the compartments improved? Which compartments are now the least well resolved from each other? **Task 3** Re-plot the curated markers on PCA and t-SNE plots, and plot the marker profiles for each compartment with `plotDist`. Do the markers now fit the data well? **Task 4** Based on what you see, would you make any further changes to the marker list? For example, are there any compartments you would combine, such as the 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits, or any remaining outliers? Discuss your reasoning with your neighbour. Remember that there is no single correct answer. ::::: {.callout-answer collapse="true"} **Task 1** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Re-run QSep on the curated markers qsep_final <- QSep(object = msn, fcol = "markers") qsep_final ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Object of class 'QSep'. Data: msn With 13 sub-cellular clusters. ``` ::: ::: **Task 2** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Compare normalised QSep scores before and after curation par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot(x = qsep_res, norm = TRUE) title("Initial markers") plot(x = qsep_final, norm = TRUE) title("Curated markers") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P2_02_marker_annotation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Pairwise normalised QSep scores for the curated markers levelPlot(object = qsep_res, norm = TRUE, main = "Normalised QSep values for the inital markers") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P2_02_marker_annotation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Pairwise normalised QSep scores for the curated markers levelPlot(object = qsep_final, norm = TRUE, main = "Normalised QSep values for curated markers") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P2_02_marker_annotation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Removing the actin cytoskeleton class and the outlying endosomal and lysosomal markers should give similar, or slightly higher, QSep scores for the remaining compartments. Because normalised scores depend on how tight each reference cluster is, removing a few outliers from a compartment can increase the scores of that compartment. The ribosomal subunits are likely to remain the least well separated pair. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Lysosome average QSep values initial markers qsep_res@xnorm["Lysosome", ] |> median() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.543174 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ## Lysosome average QSep values after curation of markers qsep_final@xnorm["Lysosome", ] |> median() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4.077058 ``` ::: ::: **Task 3** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## PCA and t-SNE of the curated markers par(mfrow = c(1, 2)) plot2D(msn, method = "PCA", fcol = "markers", main = "Curated markers PCA") addLegend(msn, where = "bottomright", fcol = "markers", cex = .7) set.seed(399) plot2D(msn, method = "t-SNE", fcol = "markers", main = "Curated markers t-SNE") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P2_02_marker_annotation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Marker profiles for each curated compartment marker_organelles <- getMarkerClasses(msn, fcol = "markers") my_cols <- getStockcol() par(mfrow = c(4, 4)) for (i in seq_along(marker_organelles)) { marker_indices <- fData(msn)$markers == marker_organelles[i] plotDist(msn[marker_indices, ], pcol = my_cols[i], xlab = "Fraction", ylab = "Intensity") title(marker_organelles[i]) } ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](P2_02_marker_annotation_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: **Task 4** There is no single correct answer. Some reasonable options are: * Leave the 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits as separate classes if you are interested in distinguishing them, accepting that some proteins may be misclassified between them. * Combine them into a single "Ribosome" class to improve resolution, at the cost of finer detail. This can be done with `fDataToUnknown`, using the class names returned by `getMarkerClasses(msn)`, for example: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ## Replace the class names below with those in your data msn_test <- fDataToUnknown(msn, fcol = "markers", from = "40S Ribosome", to = "Ribosome") msn_test <- fDataToUnknown(msn, fcol = "markers", from = "60S Ribosome", to = "Ribosome") ``` ::: * Keep the marker list as it is. If the markers fit the data well and the compartments are reasonably resolved, further curation risks over-fitting. Whatever you decide, re-run `QSep` and re-plot the markers after each change, and keep a record of what you changed and why. ::::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} #### Key Points * A marker is a protein known to reside in a single subcellular niche in the system and conditions being studied. Markers are the labelled training data for supervised machine learning, so their quality directly affects the localisation predictions. * There is no universal marker list. Curation involves judgement calls that depend on the organism, cell type, conditions and data quality. Decisions should be justified, documented and revisited as needed, because the markers determine what downstream machine learning can learn. * Marker curation is iterative: select the compartments resolved in the data, start from an existing marker list (e.g. from `pRolocmarkers()` or a publication), evaluate it against the data, refine it and reclassify. * Aim for enough markers per class to support cross-validation (around 10–15) and, where possible, more markers than quantitative channels. Some small organelles, such as the peroxisome, may not reach this. * PCA shows only two components at a time, so check several components (`dims`) before concluding that compartments overlap. Dimensionality reduction is only a visualisation: classifiers are trained on the marker correlation profiles, so always inspect these with `plotDist()`. * `QSep()` quantifies how well compartments are separated. Normalised scores account for how tight each cluster is. A compartment is only as well resolved as its lowest pairwise score, so poorly separated compartments may need to be combined (e.g. 40S and 60S ribosome into "Ribosome") or removed. * Remove clear outlier markers, but avoid over-curation: some noise is expected, and unrealistically tight marker sets give inflated QSep scores and can lead to over-fitting of the classifier. :::
